name: Treaty with the Quapaw, 1818
aka: Treaty of St. Louis with the Quapaw, 1818
promises: A reservation between the Arkansas, Ouachita and Saline rivers kept for the Quapaw, to be surveyed at federal expense (Article 2).
The Quapaw could hunt in the ceded territory until the United States assigned it to other friendly Indians (Article 3).
No citizen of the United States or anyone else would be allowed to settle on the reserved lands (Article 4).
$4,000 in goods at signing and $1,000 in goods every year (Article 5).
Indemnity for property stolen from the Quapaw by United States citizens (Article 6).
landTaken: The Indian Claims Commission found that the area ceded east of the 100th meridian, outside the reserve, comprised 43,520,888.24 acres, and the reserve 1,163,604.75 acres (Docket 14 findings, 1951).
compensation: The Indian Claims Commission found that at the time of this treaty the Quapaw did not actually occupy and exclusively possess any part of the 43,520,888.24 acres ceded outside the reserve, and dismissed that part of the claim. It made its award instead for the reserve itself, which the Quapaw gave up six years later under the 1824 treaty (see kappler-218).
today: The reserve this treaty set aside was ceded in 1824 for a price the Commission held unconscionable; that finding is recorded under kappler-218.

nationVoice.summary: The Quapaw Nation's own history of its leader Saracen says the Nation agreed to the 1818 treaty under pressure, giving up about thirty million acres and keeping about one and a half million acres as its first reservation, and was then pressured again in 1824 into giving up the rest of its Arkansas land for a place among the Caddo on the Red River, where floods, hunger and disease followed.

openQuestions: Whether settlers entered the reserve between 1818 and 1824 in breach of Article 4 was not researched; Arkansas territorial records and the 1824 negotiation papers are the place to look.
Whether the $1,000 yearly goods under Article 5 were delivered was not researched.
The Quapaw Nation's history pages on quapawtribe.com carry no text about this treaty; a nation statement is still wanted.
2026-11-08 sweep: Court of Claims and ICC full text searched for Quapaw (no Court of Claims case) and 'Quapaw 1818', 'Quapaw August 24 1818' (ICC); nothing new beyond Docket 14, already recorded.
